question: In the spring of 2023, the Commission presented a proposal on establishing the Act in Support of Ammunition Production (ASAP). In Article 18 of the proposed regulation, Directive 2003/88/EC (the Working Time Directive) is presented as a problem for the defence industry, which could be addressed through exemptions from some of the directive’s provisions. However, Article 18 did not survive the trilogue, and was therefore not included in the regulation adopted. With this in mind: 1.
Does the Commission still consider the Working Time Directive to be a problem for the European defence industry and, if so, does the Commission intend to do something to address it?
Does the Commission consider that the Working Time Directive also poses challenges for other sectors, or are the problems identified specific to the defence industry?
Does the Commission intend to revise the Working Time Directive?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.11.2024) The Working Time Directive 2003/88/EC1 applies to all sectors of activity and lays down minimum safety and health requirements for working time. The Directive offers significant flexibilities to establish derogations in sectors and situations where this is necessary or where provided for by collective agreement at national or regional level.

Notably, in the case of activities requiring continuity of production, which may include the defence industry, Member States can derogate from several provisions of the Directive2, provided that the workers concerned receive equivalent periods of compensatory rest or, in exceptional cases, appropriate protection3.

Under strict conditions, Member States may also allow individual workers to opt out of the 48-hour average maximum weekly working time4. The Court of Justice of the EU has moreover held that the Directive may be temporarily disapplied for certain activities in circumstances whose gravity and scale are exceptional5.

The Commission considers that these provisions provide for sufficient flexibility for the European defence industry. Article 18 of the Commission’s proposal6 leading to Regulation (EU) 2023/15257 encouraged Member States to use the flexibility as regards working time in the defence industry as provided for by Directive 2003/88/EC, without modifying it in substance.

The Commission considers that Directive 2003/88/EC allows for sufficient flexibility to accommodate the legitimate needs of the sectors to which it applies, while safeguarding workers’ occupational safety and health. It does not intend to propose a revision of the Directive.
1 Directive 2003/88/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 November 2003 concerning certain

aspects of the organisation of working time, OJ L 299, 18.11.2003, p. 9‐19 - https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2003/88/oj 2 Articles 3 (Daily rest), 4 (Breaks), 5 (Weekly rest period), 8 (Length of night work), and 16 (Reference periods). 3 Article 17 of Directive 2003/88/EC. 4 Article 22 of Directive 2003/88/EC. 5 Judgment in Case C-742/19, Ministrstvo za obrambo, ECLI:EU:C:2021:597.

6 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on establishing the Act in Support of Ammunition Production, COM(2023)237 final - https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A52023PC0237 7 Regulation (EU) 2023/1525 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 July 2023 on supporting ammunition production (ASAP), OJ L 185, 24.7.2023, p. 7-25 - https://eur-lex.europa.
